MYTH: Massage flushes lactic acid out of your legs.
FACT: It doesn't. ??

The soreness you feel a day or two after a long run is usually delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), not leftover lactic acid.

What massage CAN do: help ease that sore, tight feeling as part of a bigger recovery plan that includes rest, hydration, food and easy movement.

No magic, just good bodywork. ??

Wellness marketing loves big promises: 'detox', 'flush toxins', 'instant results'.

We've chosen not to say any of that.

On our runner page, we state plainly that massage does not flush lactic acid. Soreness after hard training is usually DOMS, and bodywork may help ease it as part of a broader plan.

Why say it? Because our clients include athletes, performers and people referred by physicians and physical therapists. They notice when someone overclaims.

Small business lesson: honest positioning builds the kind of trust that turns first visits into regular clients.

Hybrid work has changed where tension shows up.

Office days: long meetings, poor chairs, back-to-back screen time.
Home days: laptops on sofas and kitchen counters, and no walk to the train.

The result we see in the studio: necks, shoulders and lower backs that never fully switch off.

Three fixes we share with every desk worker:
1. Screen top at eye level
2. Stand and move every 30–45 minutes
3. Keep the laptop off low surfaces

Small habits, fewer complaints by Friday.
